prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from being cured when the rash faded, the patient still carried a ------- form of the virus that could reawaken in her nerve cells decades later.
explanation: 'Far from being cured' and 'could reawaken ... decades later' mean the virus is present but hidden and inactive: latent.
distractor_rationales: nascent — nascent means just beginning to develop; the virus is not new but lying dormant until it 'reawakens'.
manifest — manifest means plainly visible; the rash had faded, so nothing was visible.
jaundiced — jaundiced describes yellowed skin or a bitter outlook, not a virus hiding in nerve cells.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The new battery's capacity sounds impressive in the advertisement, but its gains over last year's model are merely -------, a two-percent improvement at best.
explanation: 'Sounds impressive ... but merely' and 'a two-percent improvement' call for a word meaning small, step-by-step gains: incremental.
distractor_rationales: monumental — monumental means huge, the opposite of 'merely' a two-percent gain.
hypothetical — the two-percent improvement is measured and real, so the gains are not hypothetical.
pivotal — pivotal means decisive; 'merely' and 'two percent at best' deny that the gains matter much.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Glaciologists had assumed the ice shelf would retreat over centuries, yet the satellite record shows a ------- collapse: ice that had stood for millennia disintegrated within a single summer.
explanation: 'Yet' reverses 'over centuries'; 'disintegrated within a single summer' means the collapse was sudden and rushing: headlong.
distractor_rationales: protracted — protracted means drawn out, which is what the scientists assumed, not what the record shows.
periodic — periodic means recurring at intervals; this was a single unprecedented event.
glacial — glacial means extremely slow, the expectation that 'yet' overturns.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the compound dissolves instantly in alcohol, it is ------- in water, so the researchers had to abandon their plan to give it to patients as a simple drinking solution.
explanation: 'Although it dissolves instantly in alcohol' sets up the opposite behavior in water, and the abandoned drinking solution confirms it will not dissolve: insoluble.
distractor_rationales: gaseous — gaseous describes a state of matter, not how a compound behaves when mixed into water; it would not explain the failed solution.
inert — inert means it does not react; a nonreactive compound could still be dissolved and drunk, so the plan would not have to be abandoned.
potable — potable means safe to drink, which would make a drinking solution easier, not impossible.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The physician warned that the drug's side effects were -------: they crept in so gradually over many months that most patients never connected their growing fatigue to the medication.
explanation: Harm that 'crept in so gradually' that patients 'never connected' it to the drug is harm that advances unnoticed: insidious.
distractor_rationales: patent — patent means plainly evident; these effects went unnoticed.
lurid — lurid means vivid and shocking; a slowly growing fatigue is neither.
hyperbolic — hyperbolic means exaggerated; the warning is that the effects are real but hidden, not overstated.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Most metals crack when struck again and again, but gold is so ------- that a single ounce can be hammered into a sheet large enough to cover a small room.
explanation: 'But' contrasts gold with metals that crack under hammering; being beaten into a huge thin sheet shows it can be shaped without breaking: malleable.
distractor_rationales: granular — granular means made of grains, which would make the metal crumble, not spread into a sheet.
opalescent — opalescent describes a milky shimmer of color and says nothing about surviving hammering.
hermetic — hermetic means airtight; it has nothing to do with being beaten thin.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Whereas the finished robot had a single button that a child could operate, the first prototype was so ------- that even its own builders needed a thick manual just to switch it on.
explanation: 'Whereas' contrasts the one-button final design; needing a thick manual just to switch it on means the prototype was bewilderingly complicated: labyrinthine.
distractor_rationales: minimalist — minimalist describes the one-button final design, the very thing 'whereas' contrasts with the prototype.
monolithic — monolithic means a single uniform block, which would be simple, not something requiring a manual.
gossamer — gossamer means light and delicate; it does not explain why the machine was hard to operate.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the comet looks ------- to the naked eye, a faint smudge easily mistaken for a distant star, a telescope reveals a glowing tail that stretches millions of kilometers.
explanation: 'Although' sets the naked-eye view against the spectacular telescope view; 'a faint smudge easily mistaken for a distant star' means it looks unremarkable: nondescript.
distractor_rationales: gargantuan — gargantuan means enormous, which is what the telescope reveals, not what the naked eye sees.
kaleidoscopic — kaleidoscopic means brightly multicolored and changing; a faint smudge is neither.
incandescent — incandescent means glowing brilliantly, the opposite of a faint smudge.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The programmer's patch proved merely -------: the crashes stopped for a week, but because the memory leak causing them was never found, they returned as soon as traffic doubled.
explanation: A fix that quiets the symptom (the crashes) for a while without curing the cause (the leak) is palliative.
distractor_rationales: pernicious — pernicious means harmful; the patch did not cause damage, it stopped the crashes for a week.
holistic — holistic means treating the whole system; this patch ignored the underlying leak.
orthodox — orthodox means conventional; nothing in the sentence concerns whether the method was standard, and 'merely' plus the returning crashes point to a temporary fix.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Rather than giving every patient the same dose, the clinic now tailors treatment to each person's genes, having learned that people's responses to the drug are strikingly -------.
explanation: Dropping one dose for all ('rather than') in favor of tailoring only makes sense if responses differ widely from person to person: heterogeneous.
distractor_rationales: invariable — invariable means unchanging and uniform, which would justify one dose for everyone, the policy the clinic dropped.
gradual — gradual describes the speed of a response, not why each patient needs a different dose.
optimal — optimal means already ideal, which would give no reason to change the dosing.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Many desert shrubs look dead through the long dry season, yet they are anything but -------; within hours of the first rain they unfurl bright new leaves.
explanation: 'Look dead ... yet anything but' calls for a word meaning near death, which the quick new leaves disprove: moribund.
distractor_rationales: gnarled — gnarled means twisted and knotted; the shrubs may well be gnarled, and leafing out does not disprove it.
noxious — noxious means harmful or poisonous; the sentence is about seeming dead versus being alive.
germinal — germinal means in an early stage of growth; 'anything but' must deny the look of death, not of newness.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Though the herbal tonic was once sold as a cure for nearly every ailment, careful trials showed it to be -------, doing no more for patients than a sugar pill.
explanation: 'Though ... a cure for nearly every ailment' is reversed by 'no more than a sugar pill': the tonic has no real effect, ineffectual.
distractor_rationales: poisonous — poisonous means toxic, but a sugar pill does no harm; the comparison is about doing nothing.
palatable — palatable means pleasant to taste, which the trials of effectiveness did not address.
miraculous — miraculous is the claim the trials overturned.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Doctors long regarded damage to heart muscle as -------, but new research shows that heart cells can slowly regenerate after an attack.
explanation: 'But' sets the old view against the finding that cells 'can slowly regenerate'; the old view must have been that the damage could never be undone: irreversible.
distractor_rationales: gratuitous — gratuitous means uncalled-for; regeneration does not answer whether damage was necessary.
pervasive — pervasive means widespread; regrowth of cells does not contradict how far damage spreads.
illusory — illusory would mean the damage was not real, but regeneration presupposes real damage, so 'but' would make no sense.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Critics dismissed the early internet as a ------- curiosity, never guessing that within two decades it would reshape how nearly everyone shops, works, and talks.
explanation: 'Dismissed' plus 'never guessing it would reshape how nearly everyone' lives means critics saw it as something of interest only to a small group: niche.
distractor_rationales: groundbreaking — groundbreaking is praise, not a dismissal, and is what critics failed to foresee.
nefarious — nefarious means wicked; the critics' mistake was about how widely it would matter, not about morality.
menacing — menacing means threatening; 'curiosity' and 'never guessing' its reach point to unimportance, not danger.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Parents often treat a high fever as the most alarming symptom, but the pediatrician explained that a fever is usually -------, a sign that the body is fighting the infection rather than losing to it.
explanation: 'But' reverses 'most alarming'; a fever that shows the body 'fighting the infection' is serving as a defense: protective.
distractor_rationales: hallucinatory — hallucinatory describes visions; it is not what shows the body fighting infection.
malignant — malignant means dangerous and spreading, which repeats the alarm 'but' overturns.
omnipresent — omnipresent means present everywhere; the sentence explains what a fever does, not how common it is.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although its maker boasted of the robot vacuum's intelligence, its navigation was -------: it bumped the same chair leg dozens of times before finding the doorway by chance.
explanation: 'Although ... intelligence' is reversed by repeated bumping and finding the door only 'by chance': the navigation was clumsy and unskilled, inept.
distractor_rationales: masterful — masterful repeats the maker's boast, which 'although' overturns.
lyrical — lyrical means expressive like poetry; it says nothing about skill at navigating.
officious — officious means meddling and bossy; the vacuum's failure is incompetence, not interference.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Unlike the dry valley below, the mountain's windward slope is so ------- that moss coats every boulder and ferns sprout from the trunks of the trees.
explanation: 'Unlike the dry valley' plus moss on every boulder and ferns on trunks describe thick, rich plant growth: lush.
distractor_rationales: gaunt — gaunt means bare and bleak, closer to the dry valley the slope is contrasted with.
jagged — jagged describes a rough outline, which would not cause moss and ferns to cover everything.
molten — molten means melted by heat; nothing can grow on molten rock.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Engineers called the bridge's new sensors -------, since they had flagged a hairline crack months before it grew large enough for any inspector to see.
explanation: Detecting a crack 'months before' anyone could see it is perceiving a problem ahead of time: prescient.
distractor_rationales: myopic — myopic means shortsighted, the opposite of catching a problem months early.
obtrusive — obtrusive means getting in the way; the sentence is praise for early detection.
histrionic — histrionic means overly dramatic; quietly flagging a hairline crack is the opposite of a theatrical display.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Most of the island's birds scattered when the sailors landed, but the dodo, having never met a predator, was dangerously -------, waddling right up to the men who would hunt it.
explanation: 'But' sets the dodo against the birds that fled; never having met a predator, it paid no attention to danger: heedless.
distractor_rationales: gangly — gangly means awkwardly tall and thin; build does not explain walking up to hunters.
lugubrious — lugubrious means mournful; the dodo's problem was lack of fear, not sadness.
overwrought — overwrought means agitated and nervous, the reaction of the birds that fled, not of the dodo.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Before the printing press, copying a book was so ------- that a single monk might labor for a year to produce one Bible by hand.
explanation: A year of one monk's labor for one book means the work was a heavy burden: onerous.
distractor_rationales: nominal — nominal means trivial in amount, the opposite of a year of labor.
mechanized — mechanized contradicts 'by hand'.
immaterial — immaterial means unimportant; the sentence stresses how much effort copying took.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Physicists had expected the new particle to be -------, decaying within a billionth of a second, but it survived long enough to cross the entire detector.
explanation: The expectation of 'decaying within a billionth of a second', reversed by 'but it survived', is of a very brief existence: momentary.
distractor_rationales: kinetic — kinetic means relating to motion; crossing the detector is the surprise, so it cannot be what was expected.
paradoxical — paradoxical means self-contradictory; nothing was expected to be contradictory, only short-lived.
orbital — orbital means circling something; the expectation concerned how long the particle would last.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The patient insisted his cough was -------, nothing worse than the tail end of a cold, but the X-ray revealed pneumonia.
explanation: 'Nothing worse than the tail end of a cold', reversed by the pneumonia finding, means he thought it unimportant: inconsequential.
distractor_rationales: incurable — incurable is the opposite of dismissing it as a lingering cold.
gastric — gastric refers to the stomach; a cough is not a stomach complaint.
melodious — melodious means pleasant-sounding; the contrast is about how serious the cough was.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The early search engine's results were so ------- that a query about jaguars returned pages on cars, cats, and football teams alike, whereas modern engines guess which meaning the user intends.
explanation: Returning every kind of 'jaguar' page alike, contrasted with engines that 'guess which meaning the user intends', means the results failed to make distinctions: indiscriminate.
distractor_rationales: pertinent — pertinent means relevant, which pages about the wrong jaguars were not.
parochial — parochial means narrow and limited, the opposite of results ranging over cars, cats, and football.
imperious — imperious means domineering; it describes a manner, not a set of search results.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Cars of the 1950s were ------- with fuel, burning a gallon every ten miles, whereas today's hybrids stretch the same gallon across fifty.
explanation: Burning a gallon every ten miles, set against hybrids that 'stretch' a gallon, means the old cars spent fuel wastefully: prodigal.
distractor_rationales: provident — provident means careful to save for the future, which describes the hybrids, not the gas-guzzlers.
glutted — glutted means overfilled; the sentence is about how fast fuel was used, not how full the tank was.
imbued — imbued means filled or soaked with a quality; it does not describe using fuel up quickly.

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the new tariff made imported grain far costlier than the local harvest, city merchants who had long ignored nearby farmers began to ------- them, offering generous contracts months before the crops were even planted.
explanation: The tariff made local grain the merchants' best source, and 'offering generous contracts months before the crops were even planted' shows them actively seeking the farmers' favor - they woo them.
distractor_rationales: snub — 'offering generous contracts' is the opposite of rejecting the farmers
undercut — the merchants are seeking the farmers' grain, not underselling them; the tariff already made the local harvest the cheaper one
quarantine — nothing isolates the farmers; the merchants are drawing closer to them with contracts

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from securing the old dynasty, the emperor's decision to give each provincial governor a private army ------- the throne, for within a generation those governors answered to no one but themselves.
explanation: 'Far from securing' reverses the expected effect, and governors who 'answered to no one but themselves' show the throne's authority was being worn away from within - the decision subverted it.
distractor_rationales: repossessed — the decision gave power away to the governors; it did not take the throne back from anyone
safeguarded — 'far from securing' rules out protection
sanctified — making the throne holy is not the result of governors who 'answered to no one but themselves'

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The senators rushed the bill through in a single late-night session, hoping to ------- the governor's veto by passing it before he returned from abroad and could learn what it contained.
explanation: Passing the bill 'before he returned ... and could learn what it contained' is a way of getting around the veto - they hoped to sidestep it.
distractor_rationales: solicit — rushing so that he 'could learn' nothing shows they wanted no veto, not to ask for one
uphold — upholding his veto is the opposite of racing the bill past him
vindicate — nothing in their haste would prove his veto right

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the province had been promised self-rule and then denied it, its delegates were hardly the ------- partners the capital had hoped for; for a decade they stalled nearly every measure sent to them.
explanation: 'Hardly' denies the quality the capital wanted, and stalling every measure is what disproves it: the delegates were not easily led or managed - not tractable.
distractor_rationales: wizened — age is never at issue; stalling measures says nothing about how old the delegates were
solvent — finances are not mentioned; stalling measures has nothing to do with paying debts
voluble — stalling does not disprove talkativeness, so 'hardly' would have nothing in the sentence to deny

prompt: [Sentence Completion] So many coins had been clipped and shaved by dishonest traders that the currency itself became -------, and merchants began weighing every payment instead of trusting the value stamped on it.
explanation: Clipped coins caused merchants to stop 'trusting the value stamped on it' - the currency had become suspect.
distractor_rationales: vestigial — the currency is still in daily use; it has not shrunk to a leftover trace
usurious — excessive interest describes loans, and no lending is mentioned
sacrosanct — merchants no longer trusting the coins is the opposite of treating them as beyond question

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the rumor that the young king was a mere puppet of his uncle, his advisers had him sign every treaty in person before the assembled nobles.
explanation: Having the king sign every treaty himself in front of the nobles shows him acting on his own - the display was meant to rebut the puppet rumor.
distractor_rationales: validate — a public show of the king acting for himself works against the rumor, not for it
reiterate — repeating the rumor is not what a display of independence does
transcribe — signing treaties in person does nothing to write the rumor down

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because every spring flood spread a fresh layer of silt across the delta, its farms stayed ------- for centuries, while fields on the unflooded plateau above wore out within a few generations.
explanation: Renewing silt keeps the land productive, and the contrast with fields that 'wore out' confirms the delta farms stayed green and flourishing - verdant.
distractor_rationales: saline — salty soil is a kind of wearing out, so it cannot be the contrast with fields that 'wore out'
terraced — the cut of the land is not the opposite of wearing out, and fresh silt does not shape steps
torrid — scorching heat is not what fresh silt from a flood produces

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the treaty's ------- were set far beyond anything the defeated nation could pay, its economy buckled under the debt, and the bitterness that followed helped spark the next war.
explanation: Payments imposed by a treaty on a 'defeated nation', large enough to become crushing 'debt', are reparations.
distractor_rationales: stipends — a stipend is a regular allowance paid to someone for service, not a debt that crushes the payer
sinecures — paid posts that need little work are not a sum a defeated nation is made to pay
truces — a truce halts fighting; it is not an amount that can be set beyond what a nation can pay

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Rather than abolish the ancient council outright and provoke its noble members, the new king chose to ------- it, quietly shifting its powers one by one to his own ministers until only its ceremonies remained.
explanation: Moving its powers elsewhere 'until only its ceremonies remained' keeps the council in existence but pushes it out of real affairs - he sidelined it.
distractor_rationales: repopulate — the sentence moves the council's powers, not its members
subpoena — no court or summons to testify is involved
rejuvenate — stripping its powers away is the opposite of restoring its vigor

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although no law ever forbade the practice, the guild's ------- understanding that members would not undersell one another held for two centuries, enforced by nothing more than reputation.
explanation: No law stood behind it and only reputation enforced it, so the understanding was never set down in law or on paper - unwritten.
distractor_rationales: statutory — 'no law ever forbade the practice' rules out an understanding set down in law
rancorous — an agreement that held peacefully for two centuries was not bitter
quixotic — an impractical, idealistic scheme would not have held for two centuries

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the spring floods that had swept away the lower town three times in one century, the engineers cut a broad channel that carried the river's overflow harmlessly into the marshes.
explanation: A channel that carries overflow 'harmlessly' away is built to hold back the floods - to stem them.
distractor_rationales: swell — carrying the overflow away makes the floods smaller, not larger
simulate — the engineers built a real channel; they were not modelling floods
tabulate — cutting a channel is not counting or recording the floods

prompt: [Sentence Completion] After three failed harvests left nearly every farm owing more than it could ever repay, the town's moneylenders, rather than its lords, became its real -------.
explanation: When every farm is in their debt, the lenders hold the power the lords were supposed to hold; 'rather than its lords' points to rulers - sovereigns.
distractor_rationales: vassals — the indebted farmers are the dependents, not the lenders who are owed
squires — a squire is a knight's attendant; nothing in the debt makes the lenders servants
renegades — the lenders gain power through debts owed to them; they rebel against no one

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The framers deliberately divided the power to make war between the legislature and the executive, intending each branch to ------- the other's ambitions rather than to serve them.
explanation: Dividing power so that each branch works against the other's ambitions 'rather than to serve them' means each is meant to thwart the other.
distractor_rationales: underwrite — backing the other's ambitions is serving them, which 'rather than to serve them' rules out
transcend — dividing power does not lift one branch above the other's ambitions
satirize — a structural division of power is not mockery

prompt: [Sentence Completion] So thoroughly had the conquering empire ------- the local nobility, executing some and buying off the rest with titles and estates, that no revolt broke out for three generations.
explanation: Executing some nobles and buying off the rest brought them fully under control, which is why 'no revolt broke out' - the empire had subjugated them.
distractor_rationales: ransomed — the empire paid the nobles with titles and estates; it did not collect payment for them
radicalized — making the nobles extreme would cause revolt, not three generations without one
romanticized — idealizing the nobles does not fit executing them

prompt: [Sentence Completion] When the price of wool collapsed, the abbey responded with sweeping -------: it sold its outlying farms, dismissed half its laborers, and halted work on the new chapel.
explanation: The list after the colon - selling farms, dismissing laborers, halting building - is cutting back spending in response to lost income: retrenchment.
distractor_rationales: winsomeness — charm is not what selling farms and dismissing laborers shows
restitution — nothing is repaid to anyone who was wronged
virtuosity — dazzling skill is not the cost-cutting listed after the colon

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The builders aligned the temple so that sunlight reached its inner shrine on only two mornings a year, a design meant to ------- the pharaoh's claim to divine favor by making the gods seem to answer him on schedule.
explanation: Making the gods 'seem to answer him' gives the pharaoh's claim visible support - the design was meant to underpin it.
distractor_rationales: vitiate — a design that makes the gods seem to answer him strengthens his claim; it does not weaken it
sequester — the display was public; it did not hide the claim away
quantify — staging sunlight on the shrine does not measure the claim

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because his decrees took four months to reach the distant provinces, the emperor's authority there was largely -------: governors received his orders with great ceremony and then did as they pleased.
explanation: Governors who honored his orders in form but 'did as they pleased' show authority that existed on paper but not in practice - theoretical.
distractor_rationales: tyrannical — harsh, absolute rule is the opposite of governors ignoring him
rapacious — nothing describes the emperor seizing wealth; the point is that his orders were ignored
retroactive — the delay makes orders arrive late, but the colon explains they were ignored, not applied to the past

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The general's victories made him so popular with the army that the senate, rather than reward him, began to regard him with ------- and quietly moved the legions nearest the capital out of his command.
explanation: 'Rather than reward him' turns away from praise, and moving the nearby legions out of his command is a defensive step taken out of fear - trepidation.
distractor_rationales: smugness — moving legions away from him is a defensive act, not self-satisfaction
veneration — 'rather than reward him' rules out deep respect
rapture — delight does not lead a senate to strip a general of nearby troops

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Because the coastal plain lay below the level of the highest tides, the settlers who drained it had to keep their dikes in constant repair; a single neglected breach could leave whole villages -------.
explanation: Land below the high-tide line, protected only by dikes, would be under water if a dike broke - the villages would be submerged.
distractor_rationales: thatched — roofing is not a consequence of a breach in a dike
razed — villages are razed by people tearing them down, not by water through a breach
quarried — a breach lets in the sea; it does not dig stone out of the villages

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the newly conquered provinces, the emperor settled veteran soldiers in colonies along every major road, where they could watch the local population and break up any gathering before it grew.
explanation: Soldiers placed to 'watch the local population and break up any gathering' are there to keep the conquered people under control - to subdue them.
distractor_rationales: vacate — he moved soldiers in; he did not leave the provinces
redeem — he already held the provinces by conquest; nothing is bought back
sanitize — breaking up gatherings is control, not cleaning

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Although the king's new coins held barely half the silver of the old ones, his treasurers insisted they be accepted at full value; predictably, merchants ------- the old coins, melting them down or hiding them away while paying their debts only in the new.
explanation: Since both coins were worth the same by decree, merchants kept the silver-rich old coins out of circulation - 'melting them down or hiding them away' - and paid only with the new: they withheld the old.
distractor_rationales: spent — 'paying their debts only in the new' rules out spending the old coins
struck — striking makes new coins; the old coins already existed and were melted or hidden
taxed — taxing is the state's act; the merchants are keeping the old coins, not levying anything on them

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The treaty made the river the border but said nothing about the islands in its channel, an omission that seemed ------- at the time yet proved costly: the two nations quarrelled over those islands for the next hundred years.
explanation: 'Seemed ... at the time yet proved costly' sets up a contrast with a century of quarrels, so the omission must have looked minor - trifling.
distractor_rationales: sinister — an omission that already looked threatening would not contrast with its proving costly
wanton — a deliberately reckless omission would not contrast with its proving costly
scandalous — an omission already seen as shocking would not contrast with its proving costly

prompt: [Sentence Completion] To ------- the farmers whose fields had been flooded to build the reservoir, the state granted each of them land of equal size in the valley below, along with three years' freedom from taxes.
explanation: Equal land plus freedom from taxes makes up for the fields the farmers lost - the state meant to recompense them.
distractor_rationales: surcharge — freeing the farmers from taxes is the opposite of charging them extra
repatriate — the farmers are moved to the valley below, not returned to a homeland
tithe — a tithe takes a tenth from someone; the state is giving to the farmers

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from the spare canvases of her early career, the painter's late works are crowded with gilded frames, swirling cherubs, and layered ornament, an almost ------- excess that critics either adore or deplore.
explanation: The gilded frames, swirling cherubs and layered ornament, set against her earlier 'spare' canvases, describe extravagant, highly ornamented style: baroque.
distractor_rationales: chaste — chaste means plain and restrained, which is what her EARLY spare work was, not the crowded late work
jejune — jejune means dull or naive; 'excess' of ornament is the opposite of dull thinness
bucolic — bucolic means rural and pastoral; nothing about frames, cherubs and ornament concerns country life

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The coach had braced for mild disappointment after the narrow loss, but the mood in the locker room was nothing short of -------: players sat motionless, heads in hands, unable to say a word.
explanation: 'Nothing short of' pushes past 'mild disappointment' to its extreme, and motionless, speechless players with heads in hands show grief beyond comfort: disconsolate.
distractor_rationales: chagrined — chagrined is embarrassed annoyance, the mild end the sentence says the mood went far beyond
frenzied — frenzied means wildly agitated, contradicted by players sitting motionless
bemused — bemused means puzzled; nothing suggests confusion, and it is not a stronger form of disappointment

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Hardly a ------- student, Mina turned in every assignment early, color-coded her notes, and reread each chapter twice before the exam.
explanation: 'Hardly' reverses the examples: early work, color-coded notes and double rereading show great care, so she is hardly a careless, lazy student: lackadaisical.
distractor_rationales: dedicated — her habits show she IS dedicated, so 'hardly a dedicated student' contradicts the examples
fractious — fractious means unruly; the examples are about study habits, not behavior, so they give 'hardly' nothing to deny
dogged — her persistence IS dogged, so 'hardly' would contradict the evidence

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Far from ------- in her praise, the senior editor rarely offered a writer more than a brief nod and a single penciled check mark.
explanation: 'Far from' reverses the description: a brief nod and one check mark is the least praise possible, so she is far from gushing and lavish with it: effusive.
distractor_rationales: chary — chary of praise means sparing with it, which is exactly what she is; 'far from' rules it out
brusque — a bare nod IS brusque, so 'far from brusque' contradicts the description
guileless — guileless means innocent and sincere; nothing in the nod or check mark speaks to deceit, so the contrast has no point

prompt: [Sentence Completion] The director's films are ------- to an exhausting degree: a single scene may quote a silent comedy, a Renaissance altarpiece, a jazz standard, and a Korean folk tale.
explanation: Every example is a reference to another work, so the films are full of allusions: allusive.
distractor_rationales: didactic — didactic means preachy and instructive; quoting comedies and folk tales is reference, not teaching
jingoistic — jingoistic means aggressively nationalistic, contradicted by references drawn from many countries and traditions
elliptical — elliptical means leaving things out or hard to follow through omission; the scene ADDS references rather than omitting

prompt: [Sentence Completion] Once so ------- that the two captains shared a meal after every match, the rivalry between the clubs had by the decade's end grown so bitter that fans were barred from each other's grounds.
explanation: 'Once' sets the early rivalry against its later bitterness, and captains sharing a meal after every match shows friendly cooperation among peers: collegial.
distractor_rationales: bellicose — bellicose means warlike; that describes the LATER rivalry, and warlike captains would not dine together
internecine — internecine means mutually destructive, the end state the sentence contrasts with
